title: IMPACT OF SOCIAL MEDIA MARKETING AND WEBSITE QUALITY ON ONLINE PURCHASE INTENTION AMONG E-COMMERCE CUSTOMERS IN KATHMANDU VALLEY.

detail.title: IMPACT OF SOCIAL MEDIA MARKETING AND WEBSITE QUALITY ON ONLINE PURCHASE INTENTION AMONG E-COMMERCE CUSTOMERS IN KATHMANDU VALLEY.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract:
Kathmandu Valley is experiencing a fast development of e-commerce and therefore this necessitates businesses to curb the critical variables affecting the decision-making process of consumers in the online market. Two of these factors are Social Media Marketing (SMM) and Website Quality (WQ), which have become two important elements that play a vital role in shaping consumer behavior and online buying decisions. Social media has been crucial in the creation of engagement with the brand, disseminating information, and interacting with consumers, whereas the quality of an online shop website is a critical and crucial part of establishing trust, perceived risks, and user experiences.
The present study aimed to examine the influence of SMM and WQ on Online Purchase Intention (OPI) among e-commerce buyers in Kathmandu Valley. The research design adopted was that of a survey, where a structured questionnaire was sent to 275 respondents. Data obtained were computed through multiple regression analysis to test the relationship between the independent variables (SMM and WQ) and the dependent variable (OPI).
The findings showed that both WQ and SMM had a strong positive impact on OPI, website quality demonstrates a slightly greater relative influence on online purchase intention compared to social media marketing. These results underscore the need to capitalize on social media as a tool of engaging customers and also developing a Web site experience that is smooth, trustful, and easy to use. The research paper presents practice guidelines on how the e-commerce websites in Kathmandu Valley need to invest in order to increase the purchase intention through better social media and web quality.

title: From Technical Potential to Feasible Deployment: The Cost of Siting Fragmentation in U.S. Renewable Energy

detail.title: From Technical Potential to Feasible Deployment: The Cost of Siting Fragmentation in U.S. Renewable Energy
detail.abstract: Advancing global climate stabilization requires shifting the energy system from fossil fuels to renewables, with solar and wind expected to lead. In the United States, land and renewable resource potential are abundant, so the slow pace of transition is driven instead by institutional and social factors. This paper quantifies the cost of institutional fragmentation in the US renewable transition by: 1) synthesizing key institutional and social constraints on deployment, including local opposition, fragmented siting and zoning regimes, and permitting bottlenecks; 2) developing a land-energy-cost framework evaluating dual-use siting strategies and their trade-offs; 3) constructing a counterfactual "low-cost" benchmark in which a 100% renewable US system minimizes new land disturbance and total cost under relaxed institutional constraints; and 4) applying current state-level siting restrictions to this benchmark (the "current-siting-law" scenario) to quantify the resulting generation shortfall and its dollar cost. Results show that, absent institutional and social barriers, the US could reach a 100% renewable system while affecting only 0.6% of undisturbed land and cutting energy costs 11% relative to current fossil-based expenditures. Under current state siting law, however, this configuration falls short by 23% for solar and 3% for wind, costing an estimated $49.8 billion annually for solar and a net $-43.6 billion for wind after offsetting volume and price effects. Neither land availability nor system cost is thus the binding constraint on a US renewable transition; the primary barriers are institutional and social. This paper provides a first estimate of what those barriers currently cost.

title: Not in My Backyard? Housing Market Responses to the Announcement of a Nuclear Power Project
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management and Shanghai Jiaotong University

detail.title: Not in My Backyard? Housing Market Responses to the Announcement of a Nuclear Power Project
detail.abstract: This paper examines how local housing markets respond to the public announcement of plans for the Taipingling nuclear power project in Guangdong, China, before formal approval and construction. Using 742,627 existing-home listings and an intensity difference-in-differences design that exploits variation in distance to the project site, we find that a 10 percent shorter distance to the site is associated with an approximately 0.85 percent post-announcement decline in listing prices. The response is concentrated in the first year after the public announcement. Areas closer to the site also experience declines in residential population and increases in listing activity relative to more distant areas. Price declines are more pronounced in higher-end segments of the housing market. A back-of-the-envelope comparison suggests that, under benchmark assumptions, local housing-value losses exceed regional health benefits from reduced air pollution but are outweighed by total environmental benefits once climate benefits are included. These findings highlight a spatial and temporal mismatch between early, localized costs and broader, delayed benefits, helping explain why substantial aggregate benefits may not translate into local acceptance of nuclear power.

title: Adoption of Climate-Smart Agriculture Practices among Disadvantaged Groups in Makawanpur, Nepal

detail.title: Adoption of Climate-Smart Agriculture Practices among Disadvantaged Groups in Makawanpur, Nepal
detail.abstract: This study investigates the adoption of climate-smart agriculture practices (CSAPs) and the underlying socioeconomic determinants among historically disadvantaged indigenous and Dalit farming communities in the Makawanpur district of Nepal (specifically Raksirang, Manahari, and Kailash rural municipalities). Utilizing a post-positivist mixed-methods framework, primary data was gathered from 120 households selected via simple random sampling, alongside Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) and Key Informant Interviews (KIIs). Descriptive statistics and binary logistic regression models were applied to identify the factors influencing climate perceptions and practice adoption.,The findings indicate that a vast majority of smallholders are aware of changing climate parameters, such as increasing summer temperatures, erratic rainfall patterns, prolonged droughts, and delayed monsoons. The most severe climate-induced impact noted was pest and disease outbreaks (79%), followed by acute irrigation constraints. The observed adoption rates for targeted strategies were integrated farming systems (98%), crop rotation (67%), rainwater harvesting (52%), improved climate-tolerant crop varieties (47%), and soil/water conservation strategies (19%).,Binary logistic regression analysis revealed that institutional access to agricultural extension services significantly increased the likelihood of adopting crop rotation (β = 0.05), rainwater harvesting (β = 0.70), climate-tolerant crop varieties (β = 0.82), and soil/water conservation measures (β = 0.30). Other vital determinants included the household head's age, formal education level, gender, household income, farming experience, and ethnic background. Smallholders demonstrated a distinct preference for low-cost, high-benefit strategies. Strengthening localized climate information services and equity-focused agricultural extension systems is essential to scale up CSA adoption and support food security within marginalized mountain agrarian communities.

title: Multi-regional malaria incidence forecasting in sub-Saharan Africa: A 25-year eco-climatic benchmark using interpretable and uncertainty-aware machine learning
affiliations: Jaume I University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Multi-regional malaria incidence forecasting in sub-Saharan Africa: A 25-year eco-climatic benchmark using interpretable and uncertainty-aware machine learning
detail.abstract: Forecasting malaria dynamics across heterogeneous landscapes requires integrating non-linear climate forcing, spatio-temporal persistence, and distribution-free uncertainty quantification. We present a multi-regional eco-epidemiological benchmark for malaria incidence forecasting across 340 administrative regions in 20 sub-Saharan African countries over a 25-year period (2000–2024). We evaluated nine distinct modeling architectures, spanning statistical panel models (ARIMA, Generalized Additive Model, Mixed-Effects), tree-based ensembles (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM), and deep sequential neural networks (Long Short-Term Memory, Gated Recurrent Units, Temporal Transformer), coupled with Split Conformal Prediction (95% nominal coverage) and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (SHAP and Partial Dependence Plots). Long Short-TermMemory achieved top-tier performance in overall error variance reduction (RMSE = 19.62, R2 = 0.9689), while Mixed-Effects models minimized absolute errors (MAE = 13.66). Diebold-Mariano and Wilcoxon tests confirmed no statistically significant performance differences among top-tier architectures (LSTM, GAM, Mixed-Effects, LightGBM; 𝛼 = 0.05). Stratified eco-climatic analyses revealed that GatedRecurrent Units excelled in seasonal Arid/Sahelian zones, whereas LightGBM led in topographically complex Transitional/Highland regions (RMSE = 17.91). Mechanistic interpretability demonstrated that while historical incidence dominates predictions, climatic drivers isolate non-linear thermal optimal windows (22◦C–29◦C, peaking at 24◦C–27◦C), relative humidity operational thresholds, and hydrological saturation limits. Furthermore, lightweight architectures (GAM, Mixed-Effects, LightGBM) yielded superior conformal prediction interval efficiency (Mean Prediction Interval Width ≤132.66) with > 98.9% empirical coverage. Beyond point estimates, operationalizing the upper conformal bound (𝑌̂ upper) as a risk-averse epidemic threshold establishes an empirically grounded, distribution-free early warning trigger, enabling robust resource allocation, proactive vector control staging, and stock management within One Health surveillance systems.

title: Geopolitical Conflict and the Brent–WTI Benchmark Price Differential

detail.title: Geopolitical Conflict and the Brent–WTI Benchmark Price Differential
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether geopolitical conflict affects the Brent-West Texas Intermediate (WTI) price differential. It utilizes a manually compiled dataset of 47 geopolitical events from 2006 to 2026. The analysis compares geopolitical events and considers the role of location. The results show no evidence that direct oil-related conflicts produce a persistent widening of the spread. At medium and longer horizons, the estimated effects are negative. A decomposition of the two benchmarks shows that WTI tends to respond more strongly at intermediate horizons. Part of the subsequent narrowing in the spread also reflects elevated pre-event levels followed by mean reversion. The negative pattern remains when individual events and conflicts are removed from the sample. Overall, the results provide little evidence of persistent geopolitical segmentation between Brent and WTI. Instead, they are consistent with geopolitical information being transmitted rapidly across the two crude oil benchmarks.

title: Forecasting, Forward Contracting, and Retailer Performance in a Regulated Electricity Market
affiliations: Renmin University of China - School of Applied Economics, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and South China University of Technology

detail.title: Forecasting, Forward Contracting, and Retailer Performance in a Regulated Electricity Market
detail.abstract: Forecast improvements are widely expected to enhance trading performance, yet their economic value depends on how forecast information is incorporated into contracting decisions. This paper studies the interaction between spot price forecasting and forward contracting in a regulated, sequential electricity market. We first develop an integrated framework that embeds month-ahead spot price forecasts and retailer portfolio choices into a forward equilibrium model. Then, using data from China's Guangdong wholesale market, we demonstrate that while a hybrid approach combing structural modelling with machine learning substantially improves forecasting accuracy, the improvements alone do not guarantee higher profitability. Economic gains arise only when retailers can flexibly adjust forward positions in response. We further document pronounced heterogeneity across retailers of varying sizes and regulatory conditions. Overall, the results illustrate how the value of information in electricity markets is shaped by forward contracting institutions and regulatory design.

keywords: Information Processing Capacity JEL Codes: M15

detail.abstract: Biodiversity loss has become a global ecological crisis. As the primary participants in economic activities, corporations generally exhibit low levels of biodiversity information disclosure, raising widespread concern. This paper examines the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption on corporate biodiversity disclosure and its underlying mechanisms from the perspective of information processing capacity. Using data from Chinese A-share listed companies over the period 2010 to 2023, we measure firms' AI technology adoption using a machine learning approach based on the BERT pre-trained language model and construct a biodiversity disclosure intensity indicator through text analysis. The results indicate that AI adoption significantly increases corporate biodiversity disclosure intensity. Three pathways through which AI promotes biodiversity disclosure are: improving environmental information disclosure quality, enhancing energy efficiency, and strengthening environmental compliance identification capacity. Moreover, the facilitating effect of AI is more pronounced in firms with higher institutional investor shareholding, those in heavily polluting industries, and those operating in less concentrated (i.e., more competitive) industries. These findings highlight the "spotlight effect" of AI on ecological risk from an information processing capacity perspective, systematically identifying multiple transmission channels through which AI affects biodiversity disclosure, and extending the research on the economic consequences of AI to the domain of non-financial information disclosure.

title: Planning External-Data Adoption in Energy-Market Forecasting: A Matched Decision Framework for Global News
affiliations: Guangdong Medical University, Saitama University and Saitama University, Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences

detail.title: Planning External-Data Adoption in Energy-Market Forecasting: A Matched Decision Framework for Global News
detail.abstract: Energy planners must decide whether to acquire and maintain external data before knowing whether the added information will improve operational forecasts. This paper develops a matched decision framework that converts the forecast gain from an added feed into a model-specific break-even adoption threshold. The framework closes news windows before each forecast, holds target dates, rows, model selection, and calibration fixed, and then compares market-only (M0) with news-augmented (M1) forecasts. We apply it to nine daily energy-return series from 3 January 2020 to 17 April 2026 using traditional, domain-trained deep, and pretrained time-series models. Adding Global Database of Events, Language, and Tone news raises mean absolute error (MAE) by 0.018 for long short-term memory, 0.026 for a causal Transformer, and 0.018 for a Temporal Fusion Transformer; all three block-bootstrap intervals remain above zero after Holm adjustment. Ridge instead lowers MAE by 0.016, while the random-forest and foundation-model intervals span zero. The planning layer expresses each gain as a percentage of market-only MAE. Ridge supports adoption only when the loss-equivalent feed cost is below a robust threshold of 0.635%; the three deep models retain market-only information even at zero feed cost, and the remaining comparisons support deferral or redesign. Market-only Temporal Fusion Transformer records the lowest MAE among 16 model-information combinations, while calibration effects vary across forecast cells. By separating model selection from data-source adoption, the framework turns retrospective forecast evaluation into a prospective procurement and governance rule for asynchronous external feeds.

title: Threshold Effects of Monetary Policy on Ecological Footprint in Developing Economies: The Roles of Economic Complexity and Governance Quality
affiliations: Shiraz University and Shiraz University

detail.title: Threshold Effects of Monetary Policy on Ecological Footprint in Developing Economies: The Roles of Economic Complexity and Governance Quality
detail.abstract: The environmental consequences of monetary policy remain insufficiently understood in developing economies, where differences in economic structure and governance may shape the transmission of monetary expansion to ecological pressure. Using GMM-estimated dynamic panel threshold models for 65 developing countries (2002–2023), we assess whether the environmental effect of monetary expansion differs across regimes defined by economic complexity and governance quality. Real broad money (M2/P) is the baseline monetary measure, with the broad-money-to-GDP ratio (M2/GDP) used as a robustness check. Monetary expansion is positively associated with ecological footprint, but the strength of this association varies across structural and governance regimes. Economic complexity and governance quality each have positive direct associations with ecological footprint and serve as significant threshold conditions. In the baseline M2/P specification, the monetary-expansion coefficient is larger above both the economic-complexity and governance-quality thresholds. With M2/GDP, the complexity-threshold result is preserved, whereas the governance-threshold pattern reverses, indicating that the estimated role of governance is sensitive to how monetary expansion is scaled. Supplementary specifications, in which the monetary-policy variable itself serves as the threshold, also reveal nonlinear effects but yield different regime patterns. Ecological footprint is highly persistent, highlighting the importance of timely environmental intervention. Renewable energy, trade openness, and human capital are associated with lower ecological pressure, while economic growth increases it; economic uncertainty is insignificant, implying offsetting channels. Monetary expansion is therefore not environmentally neutral, and its implications depend on economic structure, governance quality, and measurement. These findings underscore the need to coordinate monetary, environmental, and structural policies.

title: The Effects of Conditionally Mandatory Disclosures: Evidence from Climate-Related Scenario Analysis
affiliations: Boston University - Questrom School of Business and Texas State University - McCoy College of Business

detail.title: The Effects of Conditionally Mandatory Disclosures: Evidence from Climate-Related Scenario Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no conflicts of interest to disclose.

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the McCoy Faculty Development Fund at the McCoy College of Business at Texas State University, the McCoy College of Business at Texas State University, and the Questrom School of Business at Boston University.

detail.abstract: In two experiments, we examine the effects of conditionally mandatory reporting regimes on managers' and investors' decision-making. We find that managers are less likely to undertake activities that trigger disclosure-in our setting, preparing climate-related scenario analyses-under a conditionally mandatory reporting regime than a voluntary one. This finding suggests that conditionally mandatory disclosure can discourage firms from conducting activities that give rise to disclosure. In a second experiment, we find that investors' reactions depend on both the reporting regime and industry disclosure norms. When industry norms create expectations that firms will disclose climate-related scenario analyses, investors respond more to violations of these expectations under a conditionally mandatory reporting regime than under a voluntary one. Process analyses reveal that the reporting regime and industry norms each shape investors' disclosure expectations and that their joint effect on investment interest operates through perceived management credibility. Our findings suggest that conditionally mandatory disclosure requirements have important consequences for managers and investors and may inform standard setters developing future disclosure guidance.

title: Climate risk disclosure and the cost of debt: the conditioning role of environmental performance
affiliations: Beijing Normal University - Zhuhai Campus, Beijing Normal University - Zhuhai Campus and Foshan University

detail.title: Climate risk disclosure and the cost of debt: the conditioning role of environmental performance
detail.abstract: AbstractWhether climate risk disclosure lowers the cost of debt is an open question, and the answer turns on how the average is estimated. Using Chinese listed firms over 2016-2024 (20,721 firm-year observations), we show that the average association depends on whether common time trends are absorbed: disclosure rose steadily over the period while borrowing costs fell, so part of what appears to be a disclosure premium reflects a trend rather than the price of information. What survives is conditional on credibility. The association is negative and significant for firms whose environmental performance is strong and absent for weak performers, and it is robust to alternative constructions of that split, to multiple-testing correction, and to eight different treatments of extreme borrowing costs. Neither firm size nor funding structure conditions the relation. Creditors do not reward disclosure volume; they reward disclosure that a firm's own environmental record makes credible.

title: Communicating Performance: Textual and Financial Disclosures in Private Equity
affiliations: Harvard Business School - Finance Unit,  and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.abstract: Private capital fund managers appear to possess significant information about the relative quality of their portfolio firms even within the first three years after the investment. But the way this information is disclosed to investors changes dynamically: Textual discussions of portfolio companies have substantial information about the firms' ultimate performance in the early stages of investment, while interim valuations are less important. Over time, this pattern reverses, with interim valuations becoming more important in explaining future returns, especially after portfolio companies have a financing event. The results vary not only with the tone but also with the content of fund manager disclosures. In an opaque market with substantial information asymmetries, textual discussions seem to serve as a signal about general partner quality.

title: The Costs of Meritocracy: An Agent-Based Model of Education, Inequality and Growth
affiliations: Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna di Pisa - Institute of Economics, Université de Nice Sophia Antipolis - Groupe de Recherche en Droit, Economie et Gestion (GREDEG), affiliation not provided to SSRN and Scuola Superiore Sant'Anna di Pisa - Laboratory of Economics and Management (LEM)

detail.title: The Costs of Meritocracy: An Agent-Based Model of Education, Inequality and Growth
detail.abstract: The paper develops an agent-based model to study the complex interactions between access to education, inequality and economic growth. We simulate a “meritocratic” economy where households’ ability to obtain (costly) education affects their future productivity and, in turn, their labor compensation. Simulation results show that in an economy characterized by unequal access to education and where workers are rewarded according to their productivity, income and wealth inequality surges, social mobility falls and economic growth is gradually eroded. This shows the emerging costs of meritocracy. Conversely, an institutional framework characterized by broad educational access and less meritocratic compensation schemes can foster higher and more inclusive growth. This can also be achieved introducing a policy which subsidizes education for households at the lower end of the wealth distribution. These results underscore the critical role of institutional arrangements and pre-distributive policies in promoting both equity and long-term economic performance.

title: Consumer discourse on e-commerce home-delivery overpackaging in South Korea: A longitudinal social media analytics study
affiliations: Inje University, Kyung Hee University and Pusan National University

detail.title: Consumer discourse on e-commerce home-delivery overpackaging in South Korea: A longitudinal social media analytics study
detail.abstract: PurposeThis study examines how YouTube users discuss home-delivery overpackaging in e-commerce and how this online discourse changed during a period of rapid digital commerce growth and pandemic disruption.Design/methodology/approachThe study analyses Korean-language YouTube data from 2014 to 2022, comprising 750 videos and 11,541 user comments. After text preprocessing and TF–IDF-based filtering, frequency analysis and Latent Dirichlet Allocation topic modelling were used to identify major themes in video and comment discourse and to compare their changes across three time periods.FindingsThe findings show that YouTube discourse on home-delivery overpackaging is organised around two broad concerns: environmental consequences and consumption-related experience. Video content tends to foreground eco-friendly packaging, regulation and waste issues, whereas user comments show stronger attention to recycling burden, delivery quality, product protection, packaging appearance, price sensitivity and courier labour. Over time, the discourse shifts from criticism of visibly excessive packaging to a broader discussion of sustainability, service quality and everyday handling.Originality/valueThis study contributes by examining e-commerce overpackaging through online public discourse in South Korea, a highly developed and mobile-intensive e-commerce market where home delivery is deeply embedded in everyday consumption. Rather than treating overpackaging only as an environmental or logistics issue, it shows how YouTube videos and comments create different layers of public information about sustainability, service quality, disposal burden and courier labour. The longitudinal design offers a platform-based view of how such meanings evolve over time.

detail.title: Charting the Future of Blockchain in Operations and Supply Chain Management: Opportunities and Challenges

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: This Special Issue on Operational Perspectives on Blockchain Applications presents cutting-edge research that explores blockchain's opportunities, challenges, and implications for OM. The articles in this issue provide a diverse and empirically grounded examination of blockchain applications across industries and operational contexts. We will discuss each contribution in turn. However, prior to that, it is useful to dig into the operational nuances, opportunities, and challenges presented by the focal context. Our editorial discussion opens accordingly, outlining the technological, organizational, and regulatory challenges while identifying the conditions under which blockchain can deliver value. We also touch on the broader societal implications of blockchain, addressing its political, economic, social, environmental, and legal dimensions before describing how each of the papers in the special issue contributes to understanding, critical to operations management. Finally, our editorial discussion concludes by charting a research agenda, highlighting key questions and interdisciplinary approaches needed to advance both theoretical and practical understanding of blockchain in OM.

title: Label Quality and Ground-Truth Problems in Metadata-Based Counterfeit Detection: A Critical Review
affiliations: , Government College University Lahore, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of the Punjab, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of the Punjab

detail.title: Label Quality and Ground-Truth Problems in Metadata-Based Counterfeit Detection: A Critical Review
detail.abstract: Metadata-based counterfeit detection infers whether an online offer, seller or website is associated with counterfeit goods from attributes that can be collected without handling the product, such as listing text, price, seller reputation and website registration data. These attributes are inexpensive to acquire at scale, and reported accuracies can be high; yet whether a product is counterfeit is a physical and legal property that is rarely observable when a listing is collected, so the labels used for training and evaluation are, in most cases, proxies. This review critically examines how ground truth is constructed in metadata-based counterfeit detection and how label quality conditions the interpretation of reported results. Drawing on bibliographically verified primary studies of counterfeit storefronts, marketplace offers and illicit online pharmacies, and on methodological work on label noise, weak supervision, annotation reliability, data leakage and dataset documentation, we (i) propose a taxonomy of ground-truth sources—physical authentication, rights-holder and registry determinations, platform enforcement outcomes, human judgement of listings, and heuristic or query-based rules—with their characteristic error modes; (ii) analyse dataset-construction mechanisms that can inflate reported performance; and (iii) examine, as a case study, a search-engine-derived dataset of 17,123 heuristically labelled listings on which five classifiers reported accuracies of 92.67–99.85%. We argue that such figures quantify agreement with the labelling procedure rather than with product authenticity, and we use class-specific and prevalence-adjusted metrics to show how their interpretation depends on label provenance and deployment prevalence. We close with a reporting checklist and a research agenda.

title: Stablecoin Runs and Treasury Fire Sales: Measurement and Partial Identification for Programmable Reserve Design

detail.title: Stablecoin Runs and Treasury Fire Sales: Measurement and Partial Identification for Programmable Reserve Design

detail.abstract:
A solvent stablecoin issuer may transmit a run into Treasury-market stress when redemption obligations arrive before reserves can be converted into settlement cash. This paper combines chain accounting with a conditional model of run propagation, timed reserve access and Treasury-market pressure. Evidence consists of 338 USDC-USDT issuer-weeks and validation records for a fixed 36-chain USDC registry. Its compiled residual is 4.358898 billion USDC, but technical supply events, circulation changes and fiat redemption are distinct quantities; heterogeneous event definitions and retained-evidence gaps prevent equating this aggregate with global cash redemption. The empirical pilot supplies predictive diagnostics and a marginal tail estimate, not structural causal elasticities. Under a severe two-hour reference state, full settlement without Treasury sales requires funding equal to 12.0144-18.9515% of the shocked issuer's reserves across a stated gross-to-net sensitivity range. This is $300.360-$473.789 billion in a hypothetical $10 trillion system with a 25% originissuer share. A second result separates funding objectives: recycling can reduce the capacity needed to eliminate net Treasury pressure while leaving substantial gross trading volume. Complete-run scenarios and delayed-funding tests delimit the design's feasible domain. A three-layer architecture links reserve eligibility, auditable collateral records and programmable settlement. The contribution is an auditable measurement framework and objective-specific capacity estimates, conditional on explicit legal, funding and timing assumptions.

Use of generative AI. OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex assisted with code, numerical checks, drafting, language revision and document preparation. The author directed the research and retains responsibility for reviewing the manuscript, its sources and computational outputs. AI-generated text is not used as evidence, and no AI system is listed as an author.

title: Relationship Between Mentorship Practices and College Students' Adjustment in a Private Higher Educational Institution in Batangas, Philippines

detail.title: Relationship Between Mentorship Practices and College Students' Adjustment in a Private Higher Educational Institution in Batangas, Philippines

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest in the conduct and writing of this research. Likewise, the authors have no competing interests to declare relevant to this article’s content.
declarations.funderStatement: The researchers themselves funded the research.

keywords: Private Higher Education Institution JEL Classification: I21

detail.abstract: The transition of first-year students to tertiary education introduces complex personal, social, and academic demands requiring responsive institutional support systems. This study investigated the relationship between mentorship practices and college students' adjustment in a HEI in Batangas, Philippines. Grounded in Alexander Astin's Theory of Student Involvement, the research utilized a descriptive-quantitative correlational design with 277 second-year college students across six academic departments as respondents to the study. Data were gathered using a validated online questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. Findings revealed that respondents strongly agreed that institutional mentors consistently delivered effective mentorship practices, with emotional and personal support receiving the highest rating. Students also achieved strong overall adjustment, led by familiarity with institutional policies and practices. Inferential analysis established statistically significant positive relationships across all mentorship practice dimensions and student adjustment domains, leading to the acceptance of the alternative hypothesis, with the strongest association observed between mentor communication and policy familiarity. Despite these positive outcomes, students encountered transition challenges, notably emotional stress, anxiety, time management, and workload balancing. To address these operational challenges, the researchers formulated a comprehensive mentoring program matrix. Theoretically, these findings extend Astin's framework by demonstrating that frontline administrative mentorship acts as an essential environmental input that reduces procedural friction and psychological anxiety. Ultimately, the study highlights crucial managerial implications for HEI, urging administrators to implement actionable strategies-such as standardizing 24 to 48-hour communication protocols, instituting bimonthly helpdesk days, mandating quarterly wellness workshops, and deploying centralized support directories to optimize long-term student adaptation and retention.

title: From the Subregional to the Continental Rationalising Without Dismantling Africa's Institutional Architecture Overlaps, Complementarities and a Functional Division of Labour among Subregional Organisations, Regional Economic Communities and the African Union

detail.title: From the Subregional to the Continental Rationalising Without Dismantling Africa's Institutional Architecture Overlaps, Complementarities and a Functional Division of Labour among Subregional Organisations, Regional Economic Communities and the African Union

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could have influenced, or could be perceived to have influenced, the work reported in this article.
declarations.funderStatement: No funder

detail.abstract: Africa does not suffer from a lack of regional organisations, but from an institutional architecture whose levels, mandates and responsibilities remain insufficiently ordered. Between specialised subregional bodies, economic and monetary unions, the eight Regional Economic Communities recognised by the African Union, the African Union itself and the African Continental Free Trade Area, a single state may simultaneously belong to several frameworks dealing with trade, money, infrastructure, governance or security. This institutional density is often interpreted as mere duplication. Such a reading is incomplete: overlap can also generate specialisation, bring public action closer to affected areas and allow differentiated integration. This article examines the necessity, added value and possible obsolescence of African organisations by moving from the subregional to the continental level. It argues that institutional relevance should be assessed function by function rather than globally from the wording of constitutive treaties. An organisation may be indispensable in monetary affairs, useful for infrastructure, redundant in trade rule-making and marginal in conflict management. A 2 framework distinguishing complementarity, specialisation, competition and duplication is applied to three configurations: CEMAC-ECCAS, WAEMU-ECOWAS and COMESA-EAC-SADC. The central thesis is that rationalisation should begin with a binding map of functions, capacities and results rather than the abolition of organisations. The proposed architecture rests on conditional subsidiarity: each function should be assigned to the closest level capable of performing it effectively, subject to conformity with continental norms and to a transfer procedure in cases of incapacity, paralysis or conflict of interest. The decisive question is therefore not whether Africa has too many organisations, but whether each organisation has an identifiable function, proportionate resources and measurable responsibility within a common system.

detail.abstract: This chapter discusses research on contracting in supply chain management and beyond. It examines the limitations sections of research on contracting in inter-organizational relationships (IORs) published this decade. A synthesis of contracting-related limitations reveals four major sets of issues. First, current conceptualization and operationalization of IOR contracting usually build on a fairly simplified characterization of contracts. More effort should be exerted to study a larger number and variety of provisions, in relation to distinct types of contracts, functions of contracts, and contract management. Second, more attention should be devoted to studying a larger number and variety of antecedents to and consequences of contract design and management. The need for a more systematic investigation of moderators and their effects has been repeatedly pointed out in the literature. Third, studies on IOR contracting should focus more on contract dynamics and its interplay with relational and other governance mechanisms as well as the link between contracts and their performance implications. These dynamics should be studied in relation to temporal factors, critical events and learning. Finally, it is noted that findings to date tend to have a narrow generalizability, as studies usually draw on a limited number of theories, use data from a limited number of actors, and mostly rely on subjective and perceptual data. Building on this synthesis, fruitful opportunities for future research into IOR contracting are discussed.

detail.abstract: This chapter surveys the literature on inter-organizational partnerships between social enterprises (SEs) and mainstream corporations, emphasizing how this type of collaboration differs from traditional corporate-corporate alliances. We reviewed 96 articles published between 2001 and 2025, highlighting the dynamic nature of SE-corporate partnerships by identifying four stages of collaboration development: philanthropic, transactional, integrative, and transformational. Together, these stages map a possible evolutionary pathway through which SE-corporate partnerships may vary in terms of resource reciprocity, institutional logic prioritization, value-creation ambition, and governance requirements. We show that while these partnerships hold significant potential for co-creating social and economic value, they also generate persistent challenges, including power asymmetries, performance measurement difficulties, and the risk of mission drift. We discuss how mechanisms such as boundary work, purpose work, and paradox management can serve as effective governance. Finally, we outline directions for future research of the dynamics of SE-corporate partnerships.

detail.abstract: This editorial advances a research agenda on collaborative strategy in the digital age. We discuss how Industry 4.0 technologies and digital infrastructures-APIs, cloud platforms, modular interfaces, and open standards-reconfigure representation, connectivity, and aggregation of information, shifting collaboration from firm-level choices to ecosystem architecture and governance. Organizing six themes, we highlight: (1) architecture-asgovernance and modularity; (2) data sharing, governance, and trust; (3) value creation and capture in ecosystems and coopetition; (4) algorithmic coordination and AI's reallocation of decision rights; (5) boundary redesign via industry clouds, consortia, DAOs, and joint data ventures; and (6) institutions, standards, and societal impact. We outline theoretical opportunities (e.g., dynamic openness, governance agility, trust pluralism, equity-aware surplus metrics) and empirical strategies (e.g., field and natural experiments, multilevel analyses, agent-based models). The agenda urges treating openness, control, and accountability as tunable levers to build innovative, resilient, and equitable ecosystems. Finally, we introduce the articles that address these themes in this Special Issue.

detail.abstract: Value Added Tax (Pajak Pertambahan Nilai/PPN) is one of the most significant sources of state revenue in Indonesia, yet its broad-based and multi-stage character means that, if applied without exception, it can raise the cost of essential goods, strategic sectors, and export-oriented industries. To address this, Indonesian tax law provides a set of VAT facilities that relieve certain transactions from the full burden of VAT, either by exempting them, by treating them as not collected, or by applying a zero percent rate on exports. This paper examines the concept, legal basis, and forms of VAT facilities available under Indonesian regulations, including the VAT Exempted (Dibebaskan) facility, the VAT Not Collected (Tidak Dipungut) facility, the zero rate applied to the export of goods and services, and special facilities granted in Special Economic Zones (Kawasan Ekonomi Khusus/KEK), Bonded Zones, and Free Trade Zones. This study employs a qualitative literature review approach, analyzing the Value Added Tax Law, government regulations, ministerial regulations, and academic sources. The discussion evaluates how these facilities are designed to support strategic national sectors such as food security, education, health, and export competitiveness, while also considering the effectiveness of these facilities and the challenges of administration, potential misuse, and their impact on state revenue. The findings suggest that VAT facilities remain an essential fiscal instrument for supporting priority sectors and investment, but their implementation requires strict supervision, clear quantitative criteria, and periodic evaluation to ensure that the facilities achieve their intended policy objectives without eroding the tax base.

detail.abstract: Nowadays, companies seek not only profitability but also long-term viability and social responsibility; thus, they must identify strategies that achieve these objectives. This article proposes a four-stage strategic framework: starting with PESTEL analysis, followed by SWOT analysis, then the Resource-Based View (RBV), and finally the Blue Ocean Strategy. Indeed, this research highlights the conceptual fragmentation found in management theory, where analytical tools are well-documented individually but their systematic integration remains underexplored. The article demonstrates how each stage illuminates and enriches the next, creating a cumulative analytical progression that moves from macro-environmental analysis to the creation of exceptional markets. This research enriches strategic management theory by bridging the gap between environmental determinism and strategic choice. It offers a systematic method for navigating increasingly complex and dynamic business environments, ensuring that strategy formulation is grounded in a deep understanding of external conditions and internal capabilities before leading to high-value innovation and the creation of new markets. The originality of this work lies in demonstrating that diverse conceptual perspectives, and strategic choice, firm resources, can be integrated into a coherent framework capable of incorporating varied insights while offering a crucial approach to strategy formulation, thus, advancing both academic discourse and strategic management practice.

detail.abstract: Background: Household food insecurity is an economic and social condition that can affect children even when adults shield them from reductions in intake. Objective: To reconcile national surveillance estimates with published evidence on correlates, child outcomes, and intervention pathways in the United States. Methods: This critical narrative synthesis examines USDA Economic Research Service (ERS) 2018-2024 household estimates and selected peer-reviewed studies with identifiable designs and directly relevant outcomes. Four original descriptive figures and four tables reorganize reported estimates and evidence. No new participants or unpublished data were analyzed, and the source selection is not represented as exhaustive. Results: In 2024, 18.4% of households with children were food insecure, compared with 13.7% of all households. Among households with children, 9.3% had food insecurity affecting adults only and 9.1% had insecurity affecting both adults and children; 0.9% reported very low food security among children. The 2024 national household prevalence remained statistically similar to 2023 and 2022, despite being higher than the rates observed during 2016-2021. Observational and review evidence links food insecurity to poorer behavioral, academic, and health outcomes, but residual confounding and inconsistent measurement limit causal inference. Conclusion: Separating household from child-specific exposure and distinguishing transient from persistent insecurity are necessary for interpreting the literature and designing stronger evaluations of food assistance. AI assistance was used in drafting, visualizing, and organizing this manuscript; the named author is responsible for verifying and approving the final content.

title: Illiberal Peace, Spatial Justice and Palestinian Political Agency in Gaza A Comparative Inquiry with Turkey's Kurdish Question and Post Conflict Societies
affiliations: National Defence College, Nigeria

detail.title: Illiberal Peace, Spatial Justice and Palestinian Political Agency in Gaza A Comparative Inquiry with Turkey's Kurdish Question and Post Conflict Societies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: This article examines Gaza as a conflict society through the concept of illiberal peace and asks whether a postwar order built principally around security management, externally controlled reconstruction and restricted political representation can produce durable peace. It develops a qualitative, comparative analysis of Gaza, Turkey's Kurdish question, Colombia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Basque Country. The study triangulates official United Nations documents, humanitarian and reconstruction assessments, legal materials, and peer-reviewed scholarship published between 2018 and September 2026. It finds that the Gaza setting displays the three mechanisms associated with illiberal peace: discursive control over legitimate political representation and the language of security; spatial control through displacement, access restrictions and the reshaping of lived landscapes; and economic control through the conditional allocation of relief and reconstruction resources. The New York Declaration of 2025 offers an important diplomatic commitment to a twostate outcome and condemnation of attacks on civilians, but it does not by itself resolve the central problem of Palestinian political agency, accountability or the material conditions of return and repair. The comparison with the Kurdish question cautions that disarmament, elite negotiation and administrative normalisation can contain violence while leaving collective grievances, memory claims and democratic participation unresolved. The article argues that an alternative cannot be reduced to a conventional liberal-peace template. A just post-iliberal future requires Palestinian-led political representation, civilian protection, truth and missing-persons mechanisms, restitution and housing rights, locally accountable reconstruction, and security arrangements constrained by law. The article contributes to the symposium's debate by connecting illiberal peace to the material landscape of Gaza and by specifying institutional tests through which external actors can distinguish conflict management from a peace capable of social repair.

title: Quantitative Modeling of EUR/USD Exchange Rate Volatility

detail.title: Quantitative Modeling of EUR/USD Exchange Rate Volatility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationship with any person or organization that could be perceived to have influenced this study. This is independent academic research conducted without external involvement.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study relies exclusively on publicly available secondary market data (FRED, DEXUSEU) and does not involve human participants, patients, or personally identifiable information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author as part of personal academic work.

detail.abstract: This document brings together the entirety of a quantitative modelling project on EUR/USD exchange rate volatility, conducted in two stages: (a) measuring, in a statistically testable way, a shift in market volatility, rather than describing it qualitatively; (b) deriving an operational use from it-a price range adjusted to the market regime and real-time regime detection. A GARCH(1,1) with Student's t innovations (ν ≈ 7,04) is specified and validated on daily log returns (FRED, DEXUSEU, 2010-2026, n = 4 175). The model's temporal stability is tested over five equal sub-periods: point estimates vary, but a likelihood-ratio test does not reject the hypothesis of a single set of parameters (p = 0,277). A baseline regression r(t + 1) = α + β 1 ∆Y (t) + β 2 r(t) + u(t) detects no predictive power on the direction of the return, a result robust to the addition of control variables (rate differential, DXY proxy). By contrast, the level of conditional volatility σ(t) explains a significant share of the magnitude of the future return (R 2 = 0,090, p < 0,001)-a result of internal consistency of the GARCH, not a new discovery. A three-state Gaussian HMM and then a Markov-Switching GARCH (K = 2, specification of Haas, Mittnik & Paolella, 2004a) yield persistent regime detection (average durations of 72 to 404 days depending on the regime and the model). The resulting operational price range is validated by an expanding-window backtest of 3,424 one-day-ahead forecasts over 2013-2026: empirical coverage of 95.50% against a nominal target of 95% (one-sided binomial test, p = 0,919)-the project's first validation with genuine statistical power. A dedicated out-of-sample robustness test for the COVID-19 crisis (January-April 2020, model re-estimated on strictly prior data) complements this result without contradicting it. Each step is documented with its errors, corrections, and acknowledged limitations, in the interest of full methodological transparency.

title: Artificial Intelligence in International Finance: An Empirical Comparison of Traditional and Machine-Learning Models for EUR/USD Forecasting Author

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in International Finance: An Empirical Comparison of Traditional and Machine-Learning Models for EUR/USD Forecasting Author
detail.abstract: This study investigates the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning in international-finance exchange-rate forecasting. The research compares a traditional ARIMA model with Random Forest and multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural-network models for forecasting the monthly EUR/USD exchange rate. The dataset contains 192 monthly observations from January 2010 to December 2025 obtained from the Federal Reserve Board's foreign-exchange series distributed through FRED. The sample is divided chronologically into a training period covering January 2010 to September 2022 and an out-of-sample test period covering October 2022 to December 2025. Machine-learning models use the previous twelve monthly exchange-rate observations as predictors, while ARIMA is selected using AIC from a small grid of candidate specifications. Forecast performance is evaluated using MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and directional accuracy. The results show that the Random Forest model achieved an RMSE of 0.0231 and MAPE of 1.76%, while the MLP achieved an RMSE of 0.0229 and MAPE of 1.75%. These errors were lower than those of the ARIMA benchmark, which produced an RMSE of 0.1156 and MAPE of 9.71%. The findings indicate that nonlinear machine-learning models can provide useful forecasting information for EUR/USD in the examined sample, while also highlighting the importance of out-of-sample validation and the limitations of relying on historical patterns alone.

title: A Computational Comparison, with an Audit of an Earlier Reduced-Form Simulation

detail.title: A Computational Comparison, with an Audit of an Earlier Reduced-Form Simulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Independent researcher
declarations.funderStatement: Not Applicable

detail.abstract:
Working paper / preprint — not peer-reviewed.
This paper examines whether replacing a fixed, predetermined capital-income claim with an income-contingent claim proportional to current net output can improve macroeconomic stability. The analysis develops a stock-flow-consistent (SFC) model based on Godley and Lavoie’s Model BMW/BMWK and compares two financing closures: a Legacy closure in which capital income is determined by a fixed contractual return on the previous period’s balance, and a Sovereign closure in which capital income is linked to current net output through a profit-and-loss-sharing rule.

The two closures are calibrated to an identical deterministic steady state and subjected to identical demand shocks across multiple stress levels and randomly drawn structural parameter sets. The results indicate that the income-contingent closure generally reduces output volatility and the probability of negative wage income when the propensity to consume from wage income exceeds the propensity to consume from property income. The mechanism operates through the distribution of income between wages and capital income: when the two consumption propensities are equal, the two financing structures generate identical output paths. At the most extreme stress level, however, the volatility advantage disappears and reverses under a stricter volatility measure, demonstrating that the stabilising effect is conditional rather than universal.

The paper also independently re-implements and audits an earlier reduced-form Monte Carlo simulation comparing Sovereign and Legacy financial structures. The audit identifies an unequal initial public-debt assumption as a confounding factor in the earlier claim concerning interest and debt-crisis failure, corrects an internally inconsistent price-dynamics calculation, and identifies a persistent discrepancy in the reproduced debt-crisis results that cannot be resolved without the original source code.

The findings provide a narrower and more testable foundation for the broader proposed economic architecture. They do not constitute validation of the full architecture, including asset-based taxation, demurrage, sovereign-wealth buffering, or open-economy mechanisms, which are outside the formal SFC model. Instead, the paper isolates and tests one specific mechanism: whether making capital income contingent on current economic performance changes macroeconomic dynamics through the distributional channel.

Corrections, critique, and independent replication are welcome — contact mo_barakatm@yahoo.com.

title: The Cultural Foundations of State Legitimacy: Kinship Intensity and Institutional Mismatch

detail.title: The Cultural Foundations of State Legitimacy: Kinship Intensity and Institutional Mismatch

detail.abstract: Why do institutional transplants succeed or fail? I argue that formal institutions lose legitimacy when they conflict with local social structures. I compare communities within ethnic homelands partitioned by borders between Civil and Common Law. Civil Law lowers economic activity in high-kinship societies but not in low-kinship societies, implying 12.6% lower GDP per capita and aggregate losses of up to 4.7%. Geocoded surveys link this mismatch to lower state trust and civic participation. The trust deficit amounts to 1.6 crosscountry standard deviations in Sub-Saharan Africa. Text analysis of a new corpus of colonial court documents finds legal language more accommodating of customary institutions under Common Law. After Civil Law judges were appointed to Cameroon's Common Law courts in 2016, economic activity fell three times more in high-kinship communities. The results suggest that compatibility between culture and institutions affects state legitimacy and economic performance.

title: Bad Controls in Trade-Sequence Regressions: Four Catches by Pre-Specified Nulls

detail.title: Bad Controls in Trade-Sequence Regressions: Four Catches by Pre-Specified Nulls

declarations.funderStatement: No funding received for this paper.

detail.abstract: Trade-level regressions invite a family of information-timing errors that standard robustness checks do not catch: predictors that are not measurable at the target trade's own entry, and entry-measurable predictors whose coefficients are corrupted by conditioning on realised-path outcomes. This note states a two-clause admissibility rule and a null-first protocol, and documents four catches from one research programme, each an apparently publishable effect. A vol-timing loading of +2.11 pips per standard deviation at t = 3.8 reproduced at +3.75 and t = 11.2 on a GARCH martingale; a feedback effect of +9.5 pips at nine standard errors dissolved under a pre-specified static control into contemporaneous co-movement; an in-sample regime gap of +11 to +13 pips collapsed to zero walk-forward while the genuine effect survived at +22.9 pips and t = 8.8; and a same-day label was retired before publication with the result intact. The protocol is cheap, mechanical, and symmetric: it kills artefacts and passes real structure through the same gate.

detail.abstract: To address consumer concerns and demands, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) helps meet health and nutritional needs while ensuring improved product traceability and integrating cutting-edge technologies. This article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) mediates the relationship between CSR and food security. It also seeks to determine how this mediation, conditioned by the degree and nature of stakeholder engagement, impacts the export strategies of agri-food companies. The methodology employs a comparative case study approach (Yin, 2018; Patton, 2002) to contrast three distinct economic settings specifically Canada, China, and South Africa based on five key variables: AI maturity by country, the level of CSR/ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) reporting, food security, stakeholder involvement, and the resilience of agri-food supply chains. The findings reveal that stakeholder involvement not only influences the intensity of the AI-CSR-food security mediation but also creates a significant, lasting qualitative impact on agri-food export strategies.

title: Bayesian Vector Autoregression for Joint Macroeconomic Forecasting: Pseudo-Real-Time Evidence, Density Forecasts, Structural Dynamics, Scenario Analysis, and Practical Macro-Risk Use for the United States
affiliations: University of Essex, Department of Economics, Students

detail.title: Bayesian Vector Autoregression for Joint Macroeconomic Forecasting: Pseudo-Real-Time Evidence, Density Forecasts, Structural Dynamics, Scenario Analysis, and Practical Macro-Risk Use for the United States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses secondary macroeconomic data and does not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects; therefore, ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: We develop a compact Bayesian vector autoregression for joint U.S. macroeconomic forecasting using an exact-vintage pseudo-real-time design for real GDP growth, core PCE inflation, the unemployment rate, and the federal funds rate. Candidate specifications vary lag length and overall shrinkage, and a pre-specified density-first rule selects the p = 2, λ = 0.1 BVAR using average log predictive density over the primary forecast horizons. Evaluation combines density and point scores, predictive-interval and calibration diagnostics, post-selection pairwise forecast tests, and a selection-aware Superior Predictive Ability test across the complete BVAR candidate family. Average LPD differentials on the balanced sample are positive for the BVAR family relative to classical VAR(4), but the SPA test does not reject the null that VAR(4) is not inferior at the 5% level (p ≈ 0.106); this non-rejection is not evidence of equivalence. The paper also reports recursive impulse responses and forecast-error variance decompositions conditional on the maintained ordering, together with a deterministic policy-rate scenario that is mechanical rather than probabilistic or causal. Robustness checks examine alternative lag lengths, shrinkage, benchmarks, horizons, simulation counts, random-number seeds, recursive orderings, inferential choices, and posterior-mean stability. The resulting BVAR is best interpreted as an auditable macro-risk information layer: it organizes the joint macro distribution, predictive uncertainty, propagation diagnostics, and scenario departures, while asset pricing, valuation, expected returns, portfolio weights, and implementation remain separate downstream tasks.

title: Automating the Executive Layer AI, Agents and DAOs
affiliations: Dignity Alliance Massachusetts

detail.title: Automating the Executive Layer AI, Agents and DAOs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interests to declare. Work as a full time pro-bono writer and advicate
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: The corporation is a legal abstraction that combines two separable functions: governance, which sets purposes, limits, and accountability, and management, which executes within them. Advances in agentic artificial intelligence are eroding the economic rationale for the executive layer that performs the second function (information aggregation, resource allocation, coordination, and monitoring) while leaving untouched the functions that cannot be delegated: specifying values, deciding moral trade-offs, and answering for outcomes. This paper argues that AI therefore threatens the C-suite as a coordinating layer far more than it threatens governance as a legitimacy function, and that automating executive management under binding human governance is in principle structurally cleaner than the present model, in which the executive layer both executes and filters what overseers see. It proposes a design in which agent officers operate inside constitutional guardrails, deterministic capital release, and escalation triggers, under an accountable human steward, a governing council with binding authority, reserved powers, and an independent auditor with direct access to agent logs. It tests the design against evidence from healthcare, nonprofit governance, and the learning-systems literature, and identifies its principal failure modes: governance capture, vendor capture, speed mismatch, proxy optimization, and the legal requirement of natural-person officers. The paper concludes that the design is a hypothesis to be piloted, beginning with a compliance-monitoring agent that reports directly to a governing body, and not a demonstrated organizational form.

title: Quantile connectedness between Indian sectoral equities, gold, crude oil and the rupee: Time-varying spillovers and portfolio implications

detail.abstract: We study return connectedness among the Nifty 50 and seven sectoral indices, gold, Brent crude oil and the US dollar-Indian rupee exchange rate for 2 January 2013 to 25 June 2026 (inclusive), a sample period which covers demonetisation, COVID-19 pandemic, Russia-Ukraine war and tariff shock in year 2025. Using the framework of the time-varying parameter VAR (TVP-VAR) and its quantile extension, we show three main results. As shown, average total connectedness over the sample period is 53.2% and very much event driven: it peaks at 77.9% in response to COVID-19. In particular, equity sectors-led by automobiles, banking and energy-act as net shock transmitters while the rupee is the system's primary shock absorber and more mild net recipients are gold and crude oil. Second, connectedness of state variables is considerably stronger in the tails of the return distribution: total connectedness reaches 86.2% at the fifth percentile and 85.8% at the ninety-fifth percentile, nearly 35 pp above their medians (about {0}). Therefore mean-based spillover estimates significantly underestimate systemic linkages in the market states that matter most for risk management. Third, according to empirical estimates using the dynamic conditional correlation (DCC-GARCH) model, gold behaves as a diversifier rather than a hedge for portfolios-variance reductions of 46-71%, depending upon particular equity-gold cases-and short rupee (long US dollar) positions are the most effective direct short hedges against Indian equity exposure. The findings are robust to alternative forecasting horizons and forgetting factors, as well as the exclusion of the aggregate market index, and carry direct implications for investors, portfolio managers, and policymakers in emerging markets...

title: Urban Water Pollution in Agra, India: Sources, Environmental Impacts, and Management Responses

detail.title: Urban Water Pollution in Agra, India: Sources, Environmental Impacts, and Management Responses

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Urban water pollution poses a serious threat to environmental sustainability and public health in rapidly growing Indian cities. Agra, a historic urban center located along the Yamuna river, has experienced significant deterioration of surface and groundwater quality due to untreated domestic sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff, tourism-related activities, and inadequate solid waste management. This review critically synthesizes peer-reviewed research articles, Central and State Pollution Control Board reports, and international agency publications from 2000 to 2025, with special emphasis on recent studies (2021-2025), to evaluate the sources, distribution, and impacts of water pollution in Agra. The analysis highlights the consequences of organic pollution, nutrient enrichment, heavy metal contamination, and microbial load on human health, aquatic ecosystems, agricultural productivity, and socioeconomic conditions. Existing mitigation measures, including sewage treatment infrastructure, industrial effluent regulation, and policy interventions such as the National Green Tribunal directives and Namami Gange Programme, are critically examined. The review identifies major research gaps related to long-term monitoring, pollutant load quantification, health risk assessment, and governance effectiveness. The study provides a consolidated scientific foundation to support evidence-based policymaking and sustainable urban water management strategies for Agra and comparable Indian cities.
